overview: This bill would direct the Interior Department, which runs federal water projects through the Bureau of Reclamation, to study whether three proposed water supply systems in the Missouri River basin are worth building. The projects would bring drinking and industrial water to towns and rural areas: the Western Dakota Regional Water System, an expansion of the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System serving parts of South Dakota, Iowa, and Minnesota, and the Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System covering parts of South Dakota, Iowa, Nebraska, and Minnesota. For each study, the federal government would pay no more than half of the cost and no more than $10 million. For the first two, the department would report to Congress on whether the project should be built and recommend that local partners pay at least 25 percent of construction costs; the third study is optional for the department. The authority for each study ends after seven years. As of October 29, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar for a vote.
for: Supporters say many rural communities in the region struggle with unreliable or poor-quality water, and that studies with shared local costs are a careful first step before any decision to build.
against: Critics say feasibility studies can lead to large federal construction commitments later, adding to a long list of rural water projects that are already authorized but not fully funded.
